Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 1–2:

(p-206) Surat al-Hijr is Meccan, and it has ninety-nine verses.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Book and a clear Qur'an.﴾ The reference of "these" is to the verses of the surah. And "the Book" is the surah; likewise "the Qur'an." Its indefiniteness is for glorification, meaning: the verses of the one that combines being a complete Book and a Qur'an that makes clear the right guidance from error with a remarkable clarity.

﴿Perhaps those who disbelieved will wish they had been Muslims.﴾ This is when they witness the state of the Muslims at the coming of victory, or at the arrival of death, or on the Day of Resurrection. Nafi' and 'Asim read ﴿rubama﴾ with a light (tashdid-less) pronunciation. It has also been read as "rabama" with a fatha and light pronunciation, and in it there are eight dialects: the ra' with a damma and with a fatha, both with shadda and without shadda, and with a ta' marbuta (feminine ending) and without it. The "ma" is a kafa (restrictive particle) that prevents it from governing the genitive, so it may enter upon a verb. Its proper place is to precede the past tense, but since what is anticipated in the reports of Allah the Exalted is like the past in its certainty, it is treated as having that status. It has also been said that "ma" is an indefinite qualifying noun, as in the saying of the poet:

"Often the souls dislike a matter, yet in it lies a relief, like the untying of a knot."

The sense of diminishment in it is an indication that if they wished for Islam even once, they would be most deserving of hastening to it, so how much more so when they wish for it every hour. It has also been said that the terrors of the Day of Resurrection will overwhelm them, so if a moment of awareness comes to them at some point, they will wish for this. The shift to the third person in reporting their wish is like the shift in your saying: "He swore by Allah that he would certainly do it."

Leave them ﴿Leave them alone﴾: let them be. ﴿Let them eat and enjoy themselves﴾ with their worldly life. ﴿And let hope divert them﴾ and occupy them with their expectation of long lives and the continuity of their circumstances, away from preparing for the return (al-ma'ad). ﴿But they will come to know﴾ the evil of their conduct when they witness its recompense. The purpose is to make the Messenger ﷺ despair of their turning back, and to inform him that they are among the forsaken (ahl al-khidhlan), and that advising them further is occupation with what has no benefit. It also contains the establishment of proof (ilzam al-hujjah) and a warning against preferring luxury and what long hope leads to.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 4–5:

﴿Never did We destroy a town but it had a known decree (kitab ma'lum).﴾ The "known decree" is a fixed term (ajal muqaddar) written in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). The exception clause (al-mustathna) is a clause in the position of a qualifier (sifah) for "town." The original rule is that the waw (wa, "and") should not enter it, as in His saying: ﴿except that warners came to it﴾. However, because its form resembled that of a circumstantial clause (al-hal), the waw was introduced as an emphasis, to show its close attachment to the noun it qualifies.

﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay it.﴾ That is: nor can they delay beyond it. The masculine pronoun referring back to "nation" (ummah) here is due to treating the word according to its meaning (al-haml 'ala al-ma'na).(p-207)

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 6–7:

﴿And they say: "O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, you are surely mad."﴾ They addressed the Prophet ﷺ with this mockingly. Do you not see what they called him, namely their statement: ﴿Surely you are mad.﴾ A similar instance is the statement of Pharaoh: ﴿Indeed your messenger who has been sent to you is surely mad﴾. The meaning is: you are indeed speaking the words of madmen when you claim that God, exalted is He, has sent down to you the Reminder, that is, the Qur'an.

﴿Why do you not bring us⦅ لَوْ ما تَأْتِينا ⦆﴾ The particle ﴿لَوْ﴾ (law, "if/why not") has been combined with ﴿ما﴾ (ma), just as it has been combined with ﴿لا﴾ (la), to convey two meanings: the prevention of one thing due to the existence of another, and tahdid (urging, reproach).

﴿with the angels⦅ بِالمَلائِكَةِ ⦆﴾ so that they might confirm you and support you in the call, as in His statement, exalted is He: ﴿Why has not an angel been sent down to him so that he might be a warner along with him?﴾ Or it is for punishment upon our denying you, as the disbelieving nations before (them) came (with punishment). ﴿If you are among the truthful⦅ إنْ كُنْتَ مِنَ الصّادِقِينَ ⦆﴾ in your claim.

(ma yunazzilu al-malā'ikata) read with the yā' and with al-malā'ikata in the accusative, on the basis that the pronoun refers to God, may He be exalted. Ḥamza, al-Kisā'ī and Ḥafs read it with the nūn; Abū Bakr read it with the tā' and in the passive voice, with al-malā'ikatu in the nominative. It was also read tanzilu, meaning tatanazzalu. ﴿Illā bil-ḥaqq﴾: "except by way of truth," meaning a descent that is bound up with the truth, i.e., in the manner that He decreed and that His wisdom required. There is no wisdom in their coming to you in forms you could see, for that would only increase you in confusion, nor in hastening punishment upon you, for among you and among your offspring are those whose word of faith has already preceded from Us. It was also said that the truth is revelation or punishment. ﴿Wa mā kānū idhan munẓarīn﴾: idhan is a response to them and the answer to an implied condition, meaning: "Even if We sent down the angels, they would not be given respite."

﴿Innā naḥnu nazzalnā al-dhikr﴾: this is a rebuttal of their denial and mockery, and for this reason He emphasized it in several ways and confirmed it with His saying: ﴿And indeed We are its guardians﴾, meaning, from distortion, addition and omission, by making it miraculous and distinct from human speech, such that any alteration of its composition would not be hidden from the people of the language; or the negation of the entry of any flaw into it in perpetuity, by guaranteeing its preservation, just as He negated that it could be criticized on the ground that its sender was [someone other than God].

It was said that the pronoun in lahu (its) refers to the Prophet ﷺ.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 10–11:

﴿And We certainly sent (messengers) before you among the sects of the former peoples.﴾ "Sects" (firaq) of them. It is the plural of shi'ah (sect), which is a group agreed upon a path and a doctrine, derived from shaʿa, meaning he followed him. Its root is al-shiyaʿ (ash-shiyāʿ), which is small kindling wood with which large logs are set alight. The meaning is: We raised up men among them and made them messengers among their own people.

﴿And there never came to them a messenger but they used to mock him.﴾ As these people do. This is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ). The particle ma (what) for the present state is not followed except by the present tense with the meaning of the present, or by a past tense close to it, and this is on the narration of a past state.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 12–13:

﴿Thus do We insert it﴾ – We cause it to enter. ﴿into the hearts of the guilty.﴾ Al-salk (insertion) is causing one thing to enter into another, like a thread into the eye of a needle, or a spear into the one who is stabbed. The pronoun refers to mockery (al-istihza').

In this there is evidence that God brings falsehood into their hearts. It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Reminder (al-dhikr), since the other pronoun in His words ﴿they do not believe in it﴾ refers to it, and this (sentence) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from this pronoun. The meaning is: in the same manner of insertion, We insert the Reminder into the hearts of the guilty, denying it and not believing in it. Or (the phrase) is an explanation of the sentence that contains it. But this argument is weak, for the succession of pronouns does not necessarily require their agreement in what they refer back to, and it is not necessary that the sentence be a circumstantial clause from the pronoun, since it may be a circumstantial clause from the guilty. Its being an explanation of the first meaning does not contradict this; rather, it strengthens it. ﴿And the way of the former peoples has already passed.﴾ That is, the way of God regarding them, by forsaking them and inserting disbelief into their hearts; or by the destruction of those among them who denied the messengers. Thus it is a warning to the people of Mecca.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 14–15:

﴿And even if We opened for them a gate from the heaven, and they were to keep ascending through it﴾ — that is, upon these who make demands. ﴿A gate from the heaven and they kept ascending through it﴾ — ascending to it and seeing its wonders all day long, becoming certain of what they see; or the angels ascend and they witness them. ﴿They would surely say﴾ — out of their extremism in obstinacy and their casting doubt upon the truth. ﴿Our eyes have only been intoxicated﴾ — they have been blocked from seeing by sorcery, from the word sukkirat (intoxicated/dazzled), and the reading of Ibn Kathir with the lightened form (sukkirat, with tashdid removed) indicates this; or they have been bewildered, from sukr (intoxication), and the reading of the one who reads "sukirat" indicates this. ﴿Rather we are a people who have been bewitched﴾ — Muhammad has bewitched us with that, just as they said when other signs appeared. In the two words of restriction and reversal (bal, "rather") there is an indication of the decisive judgment that what they see has no reality, but is rather falsehood imagined to them by some kind of sorcery.

The commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 16–18:

﴿And We have placed in the sky constellations (burūj)﴾, twelve, differing in their forms and properties, as indicated by observation (al-rasd) and experience (al-tajriba), despite the sky's smoothness. ﴿And We have adorned it﴾ with beautiful shapes and forms. ﴿For the beholders﴾, those who take heed and draw inferences from them about the power of their Originator and the oneness of their Creator.

﴿And We have guarded them from every accursed devil﴾, so that he cannot ascend to them, whisper to their inhabitants, interfere in their affairs, or gain knowledge of their conditions.

﴿Except one who steals a hearing﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "every devil." Stealing a hearing (istiraq al-sam') means snatching it covertly. It is used as a metaphor for their brief snatching from the inhabitants of the heavens, due to the affinity between them in substance, or by inference from the positions and movements of the stars. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they were not barred from the heavens. When 'Isa, peace be upon him, was born, they were prevented from three heavens. When Muhammad (ﷺ) was born, they were prevented from all of them by meteors. Its occurrence before the birth does not undermine this, since it is possible that it had other causes. It is also said that the exception is disjunctive (munqati'), meaning: "but whoever steals a hearing." ﴿Then there follows him﴾, meaning he follows him and catches up with him.

﴿a clear flaming fire (shihāb mubīn)﴾, evident to those who see. A shihāb is a bright blazing flame of fire, and the term may also be applied to a star and to a spear because of the sheen in each of them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 19–20:

﴿And the earth – We have spread it out﴾: basatnaha (We spread it out). ﴿And We have cast into it firm mountains﴾: jibalan thawabit (firm, fixed mountains). ﴿And We have caused to grow therein﴾: in the earth, or in it and in the mountains. ﴿Of every thing weighed (mawzun)﴾: measured by a specific measure required by His wisdom; or pleasing and suitable, from their saying "kalam mawzun" (a measured/balanced speech); or what is weighed and measured, or what has a weight in matters of blessing and benefit.

﴿And We have made for you therein means of livelihood (ma'ayish)﴾: by which you live, from foods and clothing. It is also read as "ma'a'ish" with a hamza, by analogy with "shama'il." ﴿And [We have made for you] those whom you do not provide for﴾: this is coordinated with "ma'ayish," or with the position of "lakum" (for you). He means by it dependents, servants, slaves, and all others whom you suppose you provide for by a false assumption; for indeed Allah provides for them and for you. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 21:

﴿And there is not a thing but that with Us are its treasuries﴾. That is: there is not a thing but that We are able to bring it into existence and create it, many times over what has been brought into existence from it. **Commentary of al-Baydawi (*Anwar al-Tanzil*) on Surah 15, verses 22–23:**

﴿And We sent the winds fertilizing﴾, pregnant (*hawamil*). He likened the wind that brings the good of forming rain-bearing clouds to a pregnant woman, just as He likened what is not like that to the barren. Or, the winds fertilize the trees (*mulaqqihat lil-shajar*). Its counterpart is *al-tawa'ih* (the ones that strike down), in the sense of *al-mutihat* (the ones that bring down), in his saying:

*"And one who gathers what the calamities bring down."*

It was also recited as *"wa-arsalna al-rih"* (the singular "the wind") according to the interpretation of the genus (*ta'wil al-jins*). ﴿Then We sent down water from the sky and gave you drink from it﴾, meaning We made it a drink for you (*suqya*).

﴿And you are not its storers﴾, meaning: not able, not empowered to bring it forth. He negated from them what He affirmed for Himself. Or it means: not guardians of it in the pools, springs and wells. This also indicates the Wise Manager, just as the movement of the air at certain times from certain directions indicates a manner in which people benefit. For the nature of water demands that it flow downward, so its remaining still without a limit requires a specifying cause.

﴿And indeed it is We who give life﴾, by bringing life into certain bodies that are receptive to it. ﴿And cause death﴾, by removing it. He interpreted "life" as encompassing animals and plants. The repetition of the pronoun serves to indicate exclusivity (*hasr*). ﴿And We are the inheritors﴾, the remaining ones, when all creatures have died.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 24–25:

﴿And We certainly know those of you who go before (in rows), and We certainly know those who lag behind.﴾ (It means) who has gone ahead in birth and death, and who has lagged behind; or who has come out from the loins of men and who has not yet come out; or who has gone ahead in Islam and jihad and hastened to obedience, or who has lagged behind. Nothing of your conditions is hidden from Us. This is a clarification of the perfection of His knowledge, after the argument for the perfection of His power, for what indicates His power is evidence of His knowledge. It has been said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) encouraged (people) to the first row, so they crowded over it, and this (verse) was revealed. It has also been said: a beautiful woman used to pray behind the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), so some of the people moved forward so as not to look at her, and some lagged behind so as to see her, and this (verse) was revealed.

﴿Indeed your Lord – it is He who will gather them﴾ without doubt, for the recompense. The placing of the pronoun (huwa) is to indicate that He alone is the One Able and the One who takes charge of their gathering, and no other. Opening the sentence with (inna, "indeed") is to confirm the promise and to draw attention to the fact that what preceded of the indication of His perfect power and His knowledge of the details of things indicates the soundness of the judgment, as He stated explicitly in His words: ﴿Indeed, He is All-Wise﴾, of dazzling wisdom, perfect in His actions, ﴿All-Knowing﴾, whose knowledge encompasses everything.

(p-210) ﴿And We created man from clay﴾: from dry clay that gives a ringing sound (yuṣalṣilu), meaning it makes a sound when struck. It is also said that it derives from ṣalṣala, meaning it became foul-smelling, the doubled form of ṣalla. ﴿From black mud﴾: clay that has changed and turned black from a long time in contact with water. It is an attribute of ṣalṣāl, meaning it is ﴿from black mud﴾ (ḥama'). ﴿Molded﴾ (masnūn): shaped, from the "form of the face" (sanat al-wajh). Or it means set up so that it would dry and take shape, like molten jewels poured into moulds, from al-sann, which is pouring. It is as if He poured out the black mud and fashioned from it the image of a hollow human. It dried until, when struck, it rang. Then He changed it stage after stage until He perfected it, and breathed into it of His spirit. Or it means foul-smelling, from sanantu al-ḥajar 'alā al-ḥajar, when I rubbed one stone against another, since what flows between them becomes foul-smelling, and it is called al-sanīn.

﴿And the jinn﴾: the father of the jinn. It is said that it refers to Iblis. It is also permissible that it refers to the species as a whole, as is apparent in the case of "man," because the diversification of the species from one person created from one material means that the whole species was created from it. Its being in the accusative is due to a verb that explains it.

﴿We had created it before﴾: before the creation of man. ﴿from the fire of the simūm﴾: from the fire of intense heat that penetrates the pores. The creation of life in simple bodies is no more impossible than its creation in bare substances, let alone in composite bodies in which the fiery element predominates, for they are more receptive to it than those in which the earthy element predominates. His saying ﴿from fire﴾ is in view of what predominates, as in His saying ﴿He created you from dust﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 28–29:

﴿And [remember] when your Lord said to the angels: "Indeed I am creating a human being from clay, from black mud altered and molded."﴾ Remember the time of His saying: ﴿to the angels, "Indeed I am creating a human being (basharan) from clay (salsal), from black mud (hama') altered and molded (masnun)."﴾ ﴿So when I have proportioned him﴾ I have made his creation balanced and prepared him for the breathing of the spirit (al-ruh) into him. ﴿And I breathed into him of My spirit﴾ until its traces spread through the hollows of his limbs, so he came alive. The origin of nafkh (breathing) is the passage of wind into the hollow of another body. Since the spirit first attaches itself to the subtle vapor that rises from the heart, and life overflows upon it so that it flows, carrying that life through the channels of the arteries to the depths of the body, its attachment to the body was called "breathing," and the attribution of the spirit to Himself (in "My spirit") is as has passed in "al-Nisa'." ﴿So fall down to him﴾ i.e., fall prostrate before him. ﴿in prostration﴾: an imperative from waqa'a, yaqa'u (to fall).

**Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 30–31:**

﴿So the angels prostrated, all of them together﴾. He emphasized it with two emphatics (*ta'kid*, emphasis) for the sake of intensifying the generality and preventing restriction (*takhsis*, specification). It is also said that he emphasized it with *kull* (all) to indicate encompassing, and with *ajma'in* (together) to indicate that they prostrated gathered together at once. But there is a problem with this, for if the matter were so, the second would be a *hal* (circumstantial accusative) and not an emphatic.

﴿Except Iblis﴾. If it is taken as a disjunctive exception (*munqati'*), then his statement ﴿he refused to be among those who prostrate﴾ is connected to it, meaning: but Iblis refused. If it is taken as a connected exception (*muttasil*), then it is a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*), as an answer to a questioner who said: "Why did he not prostrate?"

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 39–40:

﴿He said: "My Lord, because You have led me astray,﴾ The bā' is for oath (qasam), and mā is a verbal-noun (maṣdariyyah) and its answer (jawāb) follows. ﴿I will surely make [evil] seem attractive to them on earth﴾ The meaning is: I swear by Your leading me astray, I will surely make the sins attractive to them in this world, which is the abode of delusion, like His saying: ﴿he clung to the earth﴾. There is a difference of opinion regarding whether an oath may be sworn by the acts of God Most High. It is said that the bā' is causal (sababiyyah). The Mu'tazilah interpreted the leading astray (ighwā') in relation to error (ghayy), or as causing it through His command to him to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, or by misguiding him away from the path of Paradise. They gave an excuse for God's granting him respite, and that it is a cause of the increase of his error and an empowerment over him to lead the children of Adam astray, on the basis that God Most High knew of him and of those who followed him that they would die in disbelief and come to the Fire, whether they were granted respite or not; and that in granting him respite there is an opportunity for whoever opposes him to merit greater reward. The weakness of this is not hidden from people of understanding. ﴿And I will surely lead them all astray﴾ — and I will surely drive them all to error.

﴿except Your sincere servants among them﴾ — those whom You have purified for Your obedience and cleansed of impurities, so that my scheming does not take effect upon them.

Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir and Abu 'Amr read with kasr (the sincere, al-mukhlisīn) throughout the Qur'an, meaning: those who have made their souls sincere for God Most High.

﴿He said: "This is a path [that leads] to Me, straight."﴾ It is incumbent upon Me (ḥaqq ʿalayya) to observe it. ﴿Straight﴾: there is no deviation from it. The reference (al-ishara) is to what the exception (al-istithna') implies, namely the rescue of the sincere (al-mukhlaṣīn) from his seduction; or it is to sincerity (al-ikhlaṣ), in the sense that it is a path to Me (ʿalayya), leading to reaching Me without crookedness or error. According to this, the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ). According to the first view, the statement of those who stipulate that the excepted item must be fewer than the remainder is refuted, since it would lead to a contradiction between the two exceptions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 41–42:

﴿He said: "This is a path [that leads] to Me, straight."﴾ It is incumbent upon Me (ḥaqq ʿalayya) to observe it. ﴿Straight﴾: there is no deviation from it. The reference (al-ishara) is to what the exception (al-istithna') implies, namely the rescue of the sincere (al-mukhlaṣīn) from his seduction; or it is to sincerity (al-ikhlaṣ), in the sense that it is a path to Me (ʿalayya), leading to reaching Me without crookedness or error. It has also been read as ʿalā (ʿalā), from the height of honour (ʿulluww al-sharaf).

﴿Indeed, My servants—over them you have no authority, except for those of the misguided who follow you.﴾ This is a confirmation of Iblis regarding what he excepted, and a change of the grammatical arrangement (taghyir al-waḍʿ) to exalt the sincere, and because the purpose is to explain their protection (ʿiṣma) and the severing of the claws of Satan from them. Or it is a refutation of him regarding what he implied, that he has authority over those among His servants who are not sincere, for the furthest extent of his adornment is incitement and deception, as he said: ﴿And I had no authority over you, except that I called you, and you responded to me﴾. According to this, the exception is disjunctive (munqaṭiʿ). According to the first view, the statement of those who stipulate that the excepted item must be fewer than the remainder is refuted, since it would lead to a contradiction between the two exceptions.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 43–44:

﴿And indeed, Hell is the promised place for them all﴾. It is the promised place of the deviators (al-ghawin) or of the followers (al-muttabi'in). ﴿All of them﴾ is either an emphatic (ta'kid) for the pronoun, or a circumstantial clause (hal), and the governing element (al-'amil) in it is the promise (al-maw'id), if you make it a verbal noun (masdar) with an elided genitive-governed noun (mudaf) in mind; but if you make it a noun of place (ism makan), the meaning of the annexation (al-idafah) does not allow it to govern.

﴿It has seven gates﴾: they enter through them because of their large numbers, or they are levels (tabaqat) which they descend into according to their ranks in following (the deviators). These are: Jahannam, then Laza, then al-Hutamah, then al-Sa'ir, then Saqar, then al-Jahim, then al-Hawiyah. Perhaps the specification of the number is because the gatherings of destructive things are confined to relying on sensible things and following the appetitive and irascible faculties, or because its people are seven groups. ﴿For every gate of them﴾: from among the followers. ﴿A portion apportioned﴾: set aside for him. The highest of them is for the monotheist sinners, the second for the Jews, the third for the Christians, the fourth for the Sabians, the fifth for the Magians, the sixth for the polytheists, and the seventh for the hypocrites. Abu Bakr read "juz'un" with the heavy pronunciation (bi-l-tathqil).

It was also read "juzz" (with the hamzah elided and its vowel transferred onto the zay), then pausing on it with shaddah, then treating the connected reading as the pause. "Minhum" is a circumstantial clause (hal) either from it or from the pronoun resting in the adverbial phrase (zarf), not from "maqsum," because an adjective does not govern what precedes the noun it qualifies.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 45–46:

﴿Indeed, the God-fearing (al-muttaqin)﴾ from following him (Satan) in disbelief and grave sins, for other than these sins are expiated. ﴿Among gardens and springs﴾: for each one there is a garden and a spring, or for each group of them (there are) such (gardens and springs), like His saying: ﴿And for whoever fears the standing before his Lord, there are two gardens﴾, then His saying: ﴿And besides these two, there are two (more) gardens﴾, and His saying: ﴿The description of the Garden which the God-fearing have been promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered﴾, the verse (continues). Nafi', Hafs, Abu 'Amr and Hisham read ﴿wa-'uyun﴾ (and springs), and ʿuyūn with a ḍammah on the ʿayn wherever it occurs; the rest read it with a kasrah on the ʿayn. ﴿Enter them﴾ (udkhulūhā) is understood as (preceded by) an implied "saying" (i.e., "it will be said: enter them"). Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 47–48:

﴿And We shall remove﴾ in this world, by that which joined their hearts together; or in Paradise, by making their souls content. ﴿whatever rancour is in their breasts﴾, meaning the spite that existed in the world. It is related from ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "I hope that I, ʿUthmān, Ṭalḥa and al-Zubayr will be among them." Or it means envy over the ranks of Paradise and the degrees of nearness (to Allah).

﴿as brothers﴾ is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in "gardens" (jannāt), or the subject of "enter it" (udkhulūhā), or the pronoun in "secure" (āminīn), or the pronoun attached to the noun it qualifies; the governing element in it is the meaning of the annexation (iḍāfah). The same applies to His words: ﴿upon couches, facing one another﴾. It is also permissible that both be descriptions of "brothers", or a circumstantial clause from its pronoun, because it carries the sense of "mutually sincere" (mutaṣāfīn). It is also permissible that "facing one another" (mutaqābilīn) be a circumstantial clause from the implicit element in "upon couches".

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 49–51:

﴿Inform My servants that I am the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾ ﴿and that My punishment is the painful punishment﴾. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 52–53:

﴿When they entered upon him and said, "Peace."﴾ That is, we greet you with peace (salaman), or we pronounce a greeting of peace (salaman). ﴿He said, "Indeed, we are apprehensive of you."﴾ Wajilun means fearful. This was because they entered without permission and at an improper time, and because they refrained from eating. Wajal (apprehension, wajal) is the agitation of the soul in anticipation of what one dislikes.

﴿They said, "Do not be apprehensive."﴾ It is also read "la ta'jal" (do not be hasty), from awjalahu (to cause someone to feel fear), and "wa la tuwajal," from wajalahu, with the same meaning as awjalahu. ﴿Indeed, we give you good news﴾ is a resumed sentence (isti'naf) carrying the sense of a reason (ta'lil) for the prohibition against apprehension, since one does not fear the bearer of good news. Hamzah read "nubashshiruka" with a fathah on the nun and with the letter sh lightened (takhfif), from al-bishr (joy/good news). ﴿With a boy﴾ is Isaac, peace be upon him, according to His saying: ﴿And We gave him good news of Isaac﴾. ﴿Knowing﴾ means when he reaches maturity.

(p-214) ﴿They said, "Indeed, we have been sent to a guilty people"﴾ meaning the people of Lut.

﴿Except the family of Lot﴾. If it is an exception from ﴿people﴾, it is disjunctive (*munqati'*, not included in the same category), since the ﴿people﴾ are restricted by criminality. If it is an exception from the pronoun in ﴿criminals﴾, it is contiguous (*muttasil*, included in the same category). The people and the sending both include the criminals, and ﴿the family of Lot﴾ are those among them who believed in him. The meaning seems to be: We were sent to a people who were all criminals, except the family of Lot among them, so that We destroy the criminals and save the family of Lot from among them. What indicates this is His saying: ﴿Indeed, We will save them all﴾, meaning from what the people are punished with. It is a resumption (*isti'naf*, a new independent sentence) if the exception is contiguous, and it is connected to the family of Lot, functioning as a statement, but if [the exception] is disjunctive, [the clause] is connected to the family of Lot in the manner of a report. On this basis, it is permissible that His saying ﴿except his wife﴾ be an exception from the family of Lot, or from their pronoun. On the first view, it can only be an exception from their pronoun, because the two rulings differ. Unless ﴿Indeed, We will save them﴾ is taken as a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ﴿lamunajjuhum﴾ with a light (*mukhaffaf*) pronunciation.

﴿We decreed that she would be among those who remain behind﴾, meaning those who remain with the disbelievers so that she perishes with them. Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read ﴿qaddarna﴾ here and in al-Naml with a light pronunciation. It is suspended (*ta'liq*, the blocking of the verb's effect on its object while the clause still operates) because suspension is among the special features of verbs of the heart (*af'al al-qulub*), since it includes the meaning of knowledge. It is also permissible that ﴿qaddarna﴾ be treated as if it were ﴿qulna﴾ (we said), because decreeing in the sense of judgment is a kind of saying. Its origin is placing one thing at the measure of another. Their attributing it to themselves [is because], and it is the act of Allah, glorified and exalted, due to their nearness to Him and their special relationship with Him.

﴿They said, "Rather, we have come to you with that about which they used to doubt."﴾ That is: we have not come to you with that for which you disown us; rather, we have come to you with what will gladden you and cure your heart regarding your enemies, namely the punishment with which you threatened them, and about which they used to doubt.

﴿And We have brought you the truth﴾ with certainty concerning their punishment. ﴿And indeed We are truthful﴾ in what We have told you.

﴿So travel with your family﴾ go with them by night. The two Hijazi readers read the hamza of "sara" (the hamza of wasl, the connecting hamza) with a linking pronunciation, and both forms have the same meaning. It is also read as "fasir" (﴿fasir﴾), from "sayr" (travel). ﴿at a part of the night﴾ in a portion of the night. It is said that it means its last part. The poet says:

*Open the door and look at the stars.
How many portions of the dark night are upon us!*

﴿And follow behind them﴾ be at their back, driving them on, hastening them, and keeping watch over their condition. ﴿And let none of you turn around﴾ to look at what is behind him, lest he see of the terror what he cannot bear, or lest what befell them befall him, or, meaning, let none of you turn back, and let no one lag behind for some purpose, lest the punishment strike him. It is said that they were forbidden to look back so that they would prepare their souls for emigration. ﴿And go where you are commanded﴾ to the place where God commanded you to go, which is Syria or Egypt. So ﴿go﴾ is given the object ﴿where﴾, and ﴿you are commanded﴾ refers to its omitted pronoun, by way of extension (ittisa').

﴿And We decreed to him﴾, meaning: "And We revealed to him a decreed matter," which is why the verb is construed with *ilā* (إلى). ﴿That matter﴾ is vague and is explained by what follows. ﴿That the last remnant of these people would be cut off﴾: its grammatical position (*maḥall*) is accusative as a *badal* (substitution, or apposition) for the preceding "that matter." This conveys the magnitude and seriousness of the matter. It was also read with a kasra (إنَّ), as a resumed sentence (*isti'nāf*), and the meaning is: they will be completely uprooted, down to the last of them, so that not one of them remains. ﴿At dawn﴾ means entering the morning. It is a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) referring either to "these people" or to the pronoun in *maqṭū'* ("cut off"). Its plural form follows the meaning (*ḥaml 'alā al-ma'nā*), and so ﴿the last remnant of these﴾ means "those who turn their backs upon these."

﴿And the people of the city came﴾, that is, Sodom, ﴿rejoicing﴾ at Lot's guests, hoping to take them.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 72:

﴿By your life﴾ (laʿamruka) is an oath by the life of the one addressed, and the one addressed in this oath is the Prophet, peace be upon him. It has been said that it is Lot, peace be upon him, to whom the angels said this. The implied meaning is "By your life is my oath," and ʿamr is a dialect form (lughah) for life, which is used exclusively in oaths, because the lighter form is preferred in it, since it frequently passes over their tongues.

﴿Indeed, they are in their intoxication﴾ (innahum lafī sakratihim), that is, in their misguidance, or in the intensity of their lust (ghilmah), which has removed their reason and their ability to distinguish between their error and the right course to which they are being directed. ﴿Wandering blindly﴾ (yaʿmahūn) means they are bewildered, so how would they listen to your counsel?

It has also been said that the pronoun refers to the Quraysh, and the clause is a parenthetical insertion (iʿtirāḍ).

﴿So the Shout seized them﴾, meaning a terrifying, destructive shout. It was also said that it was the shout of Jibril (ﷺ... peace be upon him). ﴿At sunrise﴾, meaning they entered the time of the sunrise.

﴿So We made its highest part its lowest﴾, the highest part of the city or the highest part of their villages. ﴿and its lowest part﴾, and it was turned upside down upon them. ﴿And We rained upon them stones of baked clay﴾, of clay that had become hardened like stone, or clay upon which was a writing from the sijjil. Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 87:

﴿And We have certainly given you seven⟩ seven verses, and these are al-Fatiha (the Opening). It is also said: seven surahs, namely the long ones (al-Tuwal), and the seventh of them is "al-Anfal" and "al-Tawba," for the two are in the ruling of one surah, and for this reason no basmala was placed between them. It is also said: "al-Tawba" alone; it is also said: "Yunus," or the seven Hawamim (surahs beginning with ha mim). It is also said: seven sheets (sahaif), and these are the sub-divisions (al-Asbaʿ). ﴿of the oft-repeated⟩ is an explanation of "the seven," and "al-Mathani" derives from repetition (al-tathniya), or from praise (al-thana'), for all of that is repeated in recitation, or its words, or its stories and admonitions, or it is praised for its eloquence and inimitability, or it praises God with what is due to Him of His supreme attributes and His most beautiful names. It is also permissible that "al-Mathani" refers to the Qur'an or to all the books of God, in which case "min" (of) is partitive.

﴿And the magnificent Qur'an⟩: if "the seven" is meant as verses or surahs, then it is the conjunction of the whole to a part, or of the general to the specific; and if it is meant as the sub-divisions, then it is the conjunction of one of the two descriptions to the other.

It is said that they are those who enjoy [this worldly life]. ﴿And lower your wing to the believers﴾, and be humble toward them and be gentle with them.

﴿And say: Indeed I am the clear warner﴾, I warn you with clear explanation and proof that the punishment of Allah is descending upon you if you do not believe.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 90:

﴿As We sent down upon the dividers﴾ [i.e.] like the punishment which We sent down upon them. It is a description of the object of "the warner" (nadhir), which has been placed in its position. "The dividers" (al-muqtasimun) are the twelve who divided the entrances of Makkah during the season of pilgrimage (mawsim) in order to deter people from belief in the Messenger (ﷺ), and so Allah the Exalted destroyed them on the day of Badr. Or [they are] the group who divided [among themselves], i.e. they swore an oath to one another (taqasamu) to raid Salih (peace be upon him) by night. It was said that it is an adjective of an omitted verbal noun (masdar) that is indicated by it.

﴿And We have indeed given you﴾: here it carries the meaning of "We sent down to you." "The dividers" are those who made the Qur'an into "parts" (ʿidin), when they said out of obstinacy: "Part of it is true, agreeing with the Torah and the Gospel, and part of it is false, contradicting them." Or they divided it into poetry, sorcery, soothsaying and "the fables of the ancients." Or [they are] the People of the Book who believed in some of their books and disbelieved in others, on the basis that the Qur'an was not what they read from their books. This would be a consolation to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). His words ﴿Do not extend your eyes﴾ etc. are a parenthetical clause (i'tiraḍ) that serves as a supplement (mumidd) to it.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 91–93:

﴿Those who have made the Qur'an into parts (ʿidhīn).﴾ ʿIdhīn is the plural of ʿiḍah (parts, pieces). Its root is ʿuḍwah, from ʿaḍḍā the sheep, meaning when he divided it into limbs (aʿḍāʾ).

It is also said that it is a form (fiʿlah) from ʿaḍaḥtuhu, meaning when I slandered him (bahattuhu). In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed the one who slanders (al-ʿāḍihah) and the one who makes herself to be slandered (al-mustaʿḍihah)." It is also said that it means sorceries (asḥār). And from ʿIkrimah: ʿaḍah means sorcery. It was made into the sound plural (jamʿ al-salāmah) to compensate for what was deleted from it, and the relative pronoun with its relative clause is an attribute of "those who divided (al-muqtasimīn)," or it is a subject whose predicate is what follows.

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾, namely the division or the attribution to sorcery, so that We will requite them for it.

It is also said that it is general, covering everything they did of disbelief and sins.

In a hadith: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) cursed the one who slanders (al-ʿāḍihah) and the one who makes herself to be slandered (al-mustaʿḍihah)." It is also said that it means sorceries (asḥār). And from ʿIkrimah: ʿaḍah means sorcery. It was made into the sound plural (jamʿ al-salāmah) to compensate for what was deleted from it, and the relative pronoun with its relative clause is an attribute of "those who divided (al-muqtasimīn)," or it is a subject whose predicate is what follows.

﴿So by your Lord, We will surely question them all﴾ ﴿about what they used to do﴾, namely the division or the attribution to sorcery, so that We will requite them for it.

It is also said that it is general, covering everything they did of disbelief and sins.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verse 94:

﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ — declare it openly (fa-jhar bihi), from "sada'a bil-hujjah" (to state the proof openly), when one speaks it aloud (jahaaran). Or: separate by it (fa-ifraq bihi) between truth and falsehood. Its root meaning is clarification and distinction. "Ma" is either a verbal (masdariyyah) or relative (mawsulah) particle, and the returning pronoun is omitted, meaning: what you are commanded with (bihi) of the laws (shara'i').

﴿And turn away from the polytheists﴾ — do not pay attention to what they say.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 95–96:

﴿Indeed, We sufficed you against the mockers﴾, by subduing them and destroying them.

It is said they were five of the nobles of Quraysh: al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, al-As ibn Wa'il, Adi ibn Qays, al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth, and al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, who went to great lengths in harming the Prophet (ﷺ) and mocking him. Jibril (peace be upon him) said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "I have been commanded to suffice you against them." He pointed to the shin of al-Walid, and an archer (nabbal, one who makes or shoots arrows) passed by, and an arrow caught on his garment. He did not bend down, out of pride at taking it, so it struck a vein in his heel and cut it, and he died. He pointed to the sole (akhmas) of al-As's foot, and a thorn entered it, so his foot swelled until it became like a millstone, and he died. He gestured toward the nose of Adi ibn Qays, and he blew out pus from it and died. And he gestured toward al-Aswad ibn Abd Yaghuth while he was sitting at the base of a tree, so he began to butt his head against the tree and strike his face with its thorns until he died. And he gestured toward the eyes of al-Aswad ibn al-Muttalib, and he went blind. ﴿Those who set up another god with Allah; but they will come to know﴾ the outcome of their affair in both abodes.

Commentary of al-Baydawi (Anwar al-Tanzil) on surah 15, verses 97–99:

﴿And We know that your breast is constricted by what they say﴾: [that is, by] the polytheism, the slander against the Qur'an, and the mockery of you.

﴿So glorify your Lord with praise﴾: resort to Allah Most High in what has befallen you, by glorifying [Him] and praising [Him]; He will suffice you and remove the distress from you. Or, ﴿glorify Him [i.e., declare Him free] from what they say﴾, praising Him for having guided you to the truth. ﴿And be among those who prostrate﴾: among those who pray. And it is narrated from him, upon him be blessings and peace: "Whenever a matter distressed him, he would resort to prayer."

﴿And worship your Lord until the certainty comes to you﴾: that is, death, for its arrival is certain for every living created being. The meaning is: worship Him as long as you are alive, and do not neglect worship for a single moment. From the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "Whoever recites Surat al-Hijr, he will have ten good deeds for each of the Emigrants, the Helpers, and those who mocked Muhammad (ﷺ)." And Allah knows best.
